title: 1 Chronicles 17:16–27
context: David’s prayer responds to Nathan’s oracle and parallels 2 Samuel 7:18–29. David sits before the LORD, marvels that God has brought him so far, confesses that there is no God like the LORD, recalls Israel’s redemption from Egypt, and asks God to establish his word forever. The Chronicler’s wording differs in places, and the prayer ends by declaring that the LORD has blessed David’s house. Both traditions read the prayer as shared ground: a humble, God-centered response that takes God’s promise as the ground of its confidence.

verses.text: Then David the king went in and sat before the LORD; and he said, “Who am I, LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
verses.arminianNotes:
David the king goes in, sits before the LORD, and asks who he is, and what his house is, that God has brought him this far. The prayer parallels 2 Samuel 7:18–29.

Arminian readers see humble wonder at undeserved grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
David begins not with requests but with astonishment. His first response is to confess his smallness.

Reformed readers see a heart that receives the covenant as pure gift. Both traditions read this as shared ground, as in the 2 Samuel 7 notes on David’s prayer.

verses.text: This was a small thing in your eyes, O God, but you have spoken of your servant’s house for a great while to come, and have respected me according to the standard of a man of high degree, LORD God.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says this was a small thing in God’s eyes, yet God has spoken of his house for a great while to come and regarded him as a man of high degree. Grace exceeds expectation.

Arminian readers see God honoring David beyond his station.
verses.reformedNotes:
The wording differs from 2 Samuel 7:19, which ends differently; the phrasing is often regarded as difficult in both books.

Reformed readers see God lifting the lowly by grace. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: What can David say yet more to you concerning the honor which is done to your servant? For you know your servant.
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks what more he can say about the honor done to his servant, since God knows his servant. Words fall short.

Arminian readers see David resting in God’s full knowledge of him as he responds in gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles adds a reference to the honor done to David where 2 Samuel 7:20 is briefer.

Reformed readers see God’s intimate knowledge of his servant as a ground of comfort. Both traditions read this as shared ground about prayer resting on God’s knowledge.

verses.text: LORD, for your servant’s sake, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, to make known all these great things.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says God has done all this greatness for his servant’s sake and according to his own heart, to make these great things known. The source is God’s heart.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious purpose freely shown toward David.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 7:21 reads “For your word’s sake”; Chronicles reads “for your servant’s sake.” The narrative does not explain the difference.

Reformed readers stress that the covenant flows from God’s own heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: LORD, there is no one like you, neither is there any God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.
verses.arminianNotes:
David confesses that there is no one like the LORD and no God besides him, according to all they have heard. Praise follows gratitude.

Arminian readers see David moving from his own house to God’s incomparable greatness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The confession of God’s uniqueness echoes Israel’s basic faith, and it appears as well in the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:22.

Reformed readers see worship centered on God’s glory. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about the one true God.

verses.text: What one nation on the earth is like your people Israel, whom God went to redeem to himself for a people, to make you a name by great and awesome things, in driving out nations from before your people whom you redeemed out of Egypt?
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks what nation is like Israel, whom God went to redeem for himself, making himself a name by great and awesome deeds in bringing them out of Egypt. Israel’s story is redemption.

Arminian readers see God’s saving acts as the ground of Israel’s identity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The wording is shorter than 2 Samuel 7:23, but both recall God redeeming Israel out of Egypt.

Reformed readers see God redeeming a people for his name. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s redemption.

verses.text: For you made your people Israel your own people forever; and you, LORD, became their God.
verses.arminianNotes:
God made Israel his own people forever and became their God. The covenant relationship is God’s doing.

Arminian readers see a corporate covenant calling Israel to faithful response, as in the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:24.
verses.reformedNotes:
The language of “your own people” and “their God” echoes covenant formulas found elsewhere in Scripture.

Reformed readers see God’s faithful commitment to his chosen people. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not use the verse to settle questions of individual election.

verses.text: Now, LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant, and concerning his house, be established forever, and do as you have spoken.
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks the LORD to establish forever the word spoken concerning his servant and his house, and to do as he has spoken. Prayer takes up promise.

Arminian readers see David asking God to do what God has freely promised.
verses.reformedNotes:
Praying God’s promises back to him is a recurring pattern in Scripture’s prayers.

Reformed readers see prayer as a means God uses to bring his promises to pass. Both traditions read this as shared ground, consistent with the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:25.

verses.text: Let your name be established and magnified forever, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies is the God of Israel, even a God to Israel. The house of David your servant is established before you.’
verses.arminianNotes:
David prays that God’s name be established and magnified forever, with the confession that the LORD of Armies is the God of Israel and David’s house is established before him. God’s name comes first.

Arminian readers see David seeking God’s glory above his own dynasty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles adds the phrase “even a God to Israel” compared with 2 Samuel 7:26.

Reformed readers see God’s glory as the goal of the covenant. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build him a house. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says God has revealed that he will build him a house, so David has found courage to pray. Promise gives boldness.

Arminian readers see revealed promise inviting confident and personal prayer, as the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:27 also shows.
verses.reformedNotes:
David does not presume; he prays because God spoke first.

Reformed readers see prayer grounded in God’s revealed will. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the relationship between God’s word and the courage to pray, without pressing the verse into a debate.

verses.text: Now, LORD, you are God, and have promised this good thing to your servant.
verses.arminianNotes:
David confesses that the LORD is God and has promised this good thing to his servant. Confidence rests on God’s character.

Arminian readers see trust placed in God’s faithfulness to his word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Compared with 2 Samuel 7:28, Chronicles does not include the phrase about God’s words being truth, though the confidence is the same.

Reformed readers see the promise as secure because God himself made it. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Now it has pleased you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, LORD, have blessed, and it is blessed forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says it has pleased God to bless his servant’s house that it may continue forever, for the LORD has blessed it, and it is blessed forever. The prayer ends in confident praise.

Arminian readers see David receiving God’s blessing gratefully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Where 2 Samuel 7:29 asks God to bless the house, Chronicles states that God has blessed it. The text does not explain the shift.

Reformed readers see blessing already secured by God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground fulfilled in Christ.
